section.heading: 8.1. Arc Length
section.paragraph: What do we mean by the length of a curve? We might think of fitting a piece of string to the curve in Figure 1 and then measuring the string against a ruler. But that might be difficult to do with much accuracy if we have a complicated curve. We need a precise definition for the length of an arc of a curve, in the same spirit as the definitions we developed for the concepts of area and volume.

image.alt: A wavy curve contains a mound, a valley and a smaller mound.

section.heading: Arc Length of a Curve
section.paragraph: If a curve is a polygon, we can easily find its length; we just add the lengths of the line segments that form the polygon. (We can use the distance formula to find the distance between the endpoints of each segment.) We are going to define the length of a general curve by first approximating it by a polygonal path (a path consisting of connected line segments) and then taking a limit as the number of segments of the path is increased. This process is familiar for the case of a circle, where the circumference is the limit of lengths of inscribed polygons (see Figure 2).

image.alt: Details There are four circles with the same radii, each containing a polygon inscribed within it such that their vertices touch the circumference of the circle. The first circle has a square inscribed within it. The second circle has a hexagon inscribed within it. The third circle has an octagon inscribed within it. The fourth circle has a regular twelve sided polygon inscribed within it.

section.paragraph: Now suppose that a curve $$C$$ is defined by the equation $$y = f(x)$$ , where $$f$$ is continuous and $$a \leqslant x \leqslant b$$ . We obtain a polygonal approximation to $$C$$ by dividing the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ subintervals with endpoints $$x_{0},x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}$$ and equal width $$\Delta x$$ . If $$y_{i} = f\left( x_{i} \right)$$ , then the point $$P_{i}\left( x_{i},y_{i} \right)$$ lies on $$C$$ and the polygonal path with vertices $$P_{0},P_{1},\ldots,P_{n}$$ , illustrated in Figure 3, is an approximation to $$C$$ .

image.alt: Details A curve and many line segments are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The curve, labeled y = f(x), resembles a wave, begins directly above the mark a on the x axis, goes up to the right, reaches a peak, goes down to the right, reaches a low point, goes up to the right and reaches a height below its earlier peak, goes down to the right, and ends directly above the mark b on the x axis. The interval a b is divided into smaller intervals of equal width corresponding to the marks a, x_1, x_2, ... x_(i minus 1), x_i, ..., b. From each of these marks, vertical line segments rise upward to meet the curve at P_0, P_1, P_2, ... P_(i minus 1), P_i, ..., and P_n, respectively. Slanted line segments connect P_0 to P_1, P_1 to P_2, and so on until P_n.

section.paragraph: The length $$L$$ of $$C$$ is approximately the length of this polygonal path and the approximation gets better as we let $$n$$ increase. (See Figure 4, where the arc of the curve between $$P_{i - 1}$$ and $$P_{i}$$ has been magnified and approximations with successively smaller values of $$\Delta x$$ are shown.) Therefore we define the length $$L$$ of the curve $$C$$ with equation $$y = f(x)$$ , $$a \leqslant x \leqslant b$$ , as the limit of the lengths of these approximating polygonal paths (if the limit exists):
$$L = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left| {P_{i - 1}P_{i}} \right|$$
where $$\left| P_{i - 1}P_{i} \right|$$ is the distance between the points $$P_{i - 1}$$ and $$P_{i}$$ .

image.alt: Details The image has four parts, each depicting the same curve. The curve begins from a point labeled P_(i minus 1), goes down to the right, concave up, reaches a low point, then goes up to the right, concave up and ends at a point labeled P_i. In the first part, a line segment connects the points P_(i minus 1) to P_i. In the second part, two line segments are drawn between the endpoints of the curve, such that the first line segment, slopes upward to the right, almost horizontal, connects P_(i minus 1) to an unlabeled point on the curve and from here another line segment, slopes upward to the right until P_i. In the third part, three line segments are drawn between the endpoints of the curve, such that the first line segment, slopes downward to the right, connects P_(i minus 1) to an unlabeled point on the curve, the second line segment slopes upward to the right from the unlabeled point to another unlabeled point on the curve, and, from the second unlabeled point, the third line segment, slopes steeply upward to the right until P_i. In the fourth part, four line segments are drawn between the endpoints of the curve, such that the first line segment, slopes downward to the right, connects P_(i minus 1) to an unlabeled point on the curve, the second line segment slopes upward to the right to another unlabeled point, from here. the third line segment slopes steeply upward to another unlabeled point, and from this point, the fourth line segment slopes more steeply upward to the right until P_i.

section.paragraph: Notice that the procedure for defining arc length is very similar to the procedure we used for defining area and volume: We divided the curve into a large number of small parts. We then found the approximate lengths of the small parts and added them. Finally, we took the limit as $$\left. n\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ .

The definition of arc length given by Equation 1 is not very convenient for computational purposes, but we can derive an integral formula for $$L$$ in the case where $$f$$ has a continuous derivative. [Such a function $$f$$ is called smooth because a small change in $$x$$ produces a small change in $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ .]
If we let $$\Delta y_{i} = y_{i} - y_{i - 1}$$ , then
$$\left| {P_{i - 1}P_{i}} \right| = \sqrt{\left( {x_{i} - x_{i - 1}} \right)^{2} + \left( {y_{i} - y_{i - 1}} \right)^{2}} = \sqrt{\left( {\Delta x} \right)^{2} + \left( {\Delta y_{i}} \right)^{2}}$$

By applying the Mean Value Theorem to $$f$$ on the interval $$\left\lbrack {x_{i - 1},x_{i}} \right\rbrack$$ , we find that there is a number $$x_{i}^{*}$$ between $$x_{i - 1}$$ and $$x_{i}$$ such that
$$f\left( x_{i} \right) - f\left( x_{i - 1} \right) = f^{\prime}\left( x_{i}^{*} \right)\left( x_{i} - x_{i - 1} \right)$$
that is,
$${\Delta y_{i}} = {f^{\prime}(x_{i}^{*})\Delta x}$$
Thus we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {\left| {P_{i - 1}P_{i}} \right| = \sqrt{\left( {\Delta x} \right)^{2} + \left( {\Delta y_{i}} \right)^{2}} = \sqrt{\left( {\Delta x} \right)^{2} + {\lbrack{f^{\prime}(x_{i}^{*})\Delta x}\rbrack}^{2}}} \\ {\phantom{\left| {P_{i - 1}P_{i}} \right|}{= \sqrt{1 + {\lbrack{f^{\prime}(x_{i}^{*})}\rbrack}^{2}}\sqrt{\left( {\Delta x} \right)^{2}} = \sqrt{1 + {\lbrack{f^{\prime}{(x_{i}^{*})}}\rbrack}^{2}}\Delta x \left( {since}\Delta x > 0 \right)}} \end{array}$$
Therefore, by Definition 1,

$$L = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{\left| {P_{i - 1}P_{i}} \right| =}\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\sqrt{1 + {\lbrack{f^{\prime}{(x_{i}^{*})}}\rbrack}^{2}}\Delta x$$
We recognize this expression as being equal to
$${\int_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1 + {\lbrack{f^{\prime}{(x)}}\rbrack}^{2}}}dx$$

by the definition of a definite integral. We know that this integral exists because the function $$g(x) = \sqrt{1 + \left\lbrack {f^{\prime}(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}}$$ is continuous. Thus we have proved the following theorem:

section.paragraph: If we use Leibniz notation for derivatives, we can write the arc length formula as follows:
$$L = {\int_{a}^{b}{\sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{dy}{dx} \right)^{2}}dx}}$$

section.paragraph: If a curve has the equation $$x = g(y),c \leq y \leq d$$ , and $$g^{\prime}(y)$$ is continuous, then by interchanging the roles of $$x$$ and $$y$$ in Formula 2 or Equation 3, we obtain the following formula for its length:
$$L = {\int_{c}^{d}\sqrt{1 + {\lbrack{g^{\prime}{(y)}}\rbrack}^{2}}}dy = {\int_{c}^{d}\sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{dx}{dy} \right)^{2}}}dy$$

section.paragraph: Because of the presence of the square root sign in Formulas 2 and 4, the calculation of an arc length often leads to an integral that is very difficult or even impossible to evaluate explicitly. Thus we sometimes have to be content with finding an approximation to the length of a curve, as in the following example.

example.heading: Example 3

list.item: (a) Set up an integral for the length of the arc of the hyperbola $$xy = 1$$ from the point $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ to the point $$\left( {2,\frac{1}{2}} \right)$$ .
(b) Use Simpson’s Rule with $$n = 10$$ to estimate the arc length.

example.paragraph: Solution

list.item: (a) We have $$y = \frac{1}{x} \frac{dy}{dx} = - \frac{1}{x^{2}}$$ and so the arc length is $$L = {\int_{1}^{2}\sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{dy}{dx} \right)^{2}}}dx = {\int_{1}^{2}\sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{x^{4}}}}dx$$

(b) Using Simpson’s Rule (see Section 7.7) with $$a = 1$$ , $$b = 2$$ , $$n = 10$$ , $$\Delta x = 0.1$$ , and $$f(x) = \sqrt{1 + 1 \slash x^{4}}$$ , we have $$\begin{array}{l} {L = {{\int_{1}^{2}{\sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{x^{4}}}}}dx}} \\ {\phantom{L} \approx {\frac{\Delta x}{3}\left\lbrack {f(1) + 4f(1.1) + 2f(1.2) + 4f(1.3) + \cdots + 2f(1.8) + 4f(1.9) + f(2)} \right\rbrack}} \\ {\phantom{L} \approx 1.1321} \end{array}$$

example.paragraph: Using a computer to evaluate the definite integral numerically, we get $$1.1320904$$ . We see that the approximation using Simpson’s Rule is accurate to four decimal places.

section.heading: The Arc Length Function
section.paragraph: We will find it useful to have a function that measures the arc length of a curve from a particular starting point to any other point on the curve. Thus if a smooth curve $$C$$ has the equation $$y = f(x)$$ , $$a \leqslant x \leqslant b$$ , let $$s(x)$$ be the distance along $$C$$ from the initial point $$P_{0}\left( {a,f(a)} \right)$$ to the point $$Q\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ . Then $$s$$ is a function, called the arc length function, and, by Formula 2,
$$s\left. (x \right) = {\int_{a}^{x}{\sqrt{1 + \left\lbrack {f^{\prime}(t)}\rbrack \right.^{2}}}}dt$$

(We have replaced the variable of integration by $$t$$ so that $$x$$ does not have two meanings.) We can use Part 1 of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus to differentiate Equation 5 (since the integrand is continuous):
$$\frac{ds}{dx} = \sqrt{1 + {\lbrack{f^{\prime}(x)}\rbrack}^{2}} = \sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{dy}{dx} \right)^{2}}$$

Equation 6 shows that the rate of change of $$s$$ with respect to $$x$$ is always at least $$1$$ and is equal to $$1$$ when $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ , the slope of the curve, is $$0$$ . The differential of arc length is
$$ds = \sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{dy}{dx} \right)^{2}}dx$$
and this equation is sometimes written in the symmetric form
$$\left( {ds} \right)^{2} = \left( {dx} \right)^{2} + \left( {dy} \right)^{2}$$

The geometric interpretation of Equation 8 is shown in Figure 7. It can be used as a mnemonic device for remembering both of the Formulas 3 and 4. If we write $$L = {\int{d}}s$$ , then from Equation 8 either we can solve to get (7), which gives (3), or we can solve to get
$$ds = \sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{dx}{dy} \right)^{2}}dy$$
which gives (4).

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Find the arc length function for the curve $$y = x^{2} - \frac{1}{8}\ln x$$ taking $$P_{0}\left( {1,1} \right)$$ as the starting point.
Solution If $$f(x) = x^{2} - \frac{1}{8}\ln x$$ , then

$$\begin{array}{rll} {f^{\prime}(x)} & = & {2x - \frac{1}{8x}} \\ {1 + \left\lbrack {f^{\prime}(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}} & = & {1 + \left( {2x - \frac{1}{8x}} \right)^{2} = 1 + 4x^{2} - \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{64x^{2}}} \\ & = & {4x^{2} + \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{64x^{2}} = \left( {2x + \frac{1}{8x}} \right)^{2}} \\ \sqrt{1 + \left\lbrack {f^{\prime}(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}} & = & {2x + \frac{1}{8x} ({since}x > 0)} \end{array}$$
Thus the arc length function is given by

$$\begin{array}{l} {{s(x)} = {{\int_{1}^{x}{\sqrt{1 + {\lbrack{f^{\prime}(t)}\rbrack}^{2}}}}dt}} \\ {\phantom{s(x)} = {{\int_{1}^{x}{\left( {2t + \frac{1}{8t}} \right)}}dt = t^{2} + \left. \frac{1}{8}\ln t \right\rbrack_{1}^{x}}} \\ {\phantom{s(x)} = {x^{2} + \frac{1}{8}\ln x - 1}} \end{array}$$
